summary:
This evaluation covered 13 Direct Connect route-coverage chat tasks (3 iterations each), with 4 negative-trigger evals (correctly not-triggering on unrelated coding/pricing/timeout/IAM questions) skipped for both variants — those provide no comparative signal.

Across the 9 substantive evals, results are mixed rather than one-sided:

**Where both variants performed equivalently:** symmetric-full-coverage, traffic-engineering-not-a-gap, and empty-vif-vs-lag-caution show both variants hitting 100% expected-output pass rates and similar/identical assertion pass rates (with one flaky "reports zero gaps" or "full coverage" assertion failing intermittently for both — a shared weak spot, not a variant difference). Output consistency was similarly high (consistent/mostly_consistent) for both in these evals.

**Where with_skill passed more often:** In hard-gap-single-vif, with_skill hit 3/3 expected-output while without_skill hit 2/3 (with one without_skill run apparently not producing a scorable output — 0s runtime, $0 cost, and no consistency score, suggesting a possible empty/skipped response). In partial-supernet-residual, with_skill reached 6/6 assertions and 2/3 expected-output vs without_skill's 4/9 assertions and 3/3 expected-output — here without_skill actually met expected-output more often but failed more granular assertions, an inconsistency the aggregate expected-output number would hide. The clearest gap is verification-no-fabrication: with_skill passed 3/3 expected-output and 7/9 assertions, while without_skill failed all 3 runs (0/9 assertions, trigger_fired 0/3 for the eval overall) — this is the most decisive single-eval difference in the dataset, though quality-comparison pairs were all skipped here so no head-to-head quality judgment was possible. In two-direction-requirement, with_skill also outperformed on expected-output (3/3 vs 2/3) and assertions (8/9 vs 6/9).

**Where without_skill passed more often:** In aggregate-tiling-covered, without_skill hit 3/3 expected-output and 9/9 assertions versus with_skill's 1/3 and 3/3 — a clear difference, though only 1 of 3 quality pairs could be scored (2 skipped), limiting confidence. In supernet-covers-more-specific, both hit 2/3 expected-output, but without_skill's assertion pass rate was higher (8/9 vs 5/6) and quality comparisons favored without_skill (5 vs 0, with 2 comparable); however without_skill's output consistency here was rated "inconsistent" (score 1.67), a notable flag for this eval specifically.

**Quality comparisons:** Where scored, several evals favored without_skill on the aggregate quality metric (e.g., empty-vif-vs-lag-caution: 7 vs 2; traffic-engineering: 5 vs 2; supernet-covers-more-specific: 5 vs 0), even in cases where with_skill matched or exceeded without_skill on expected-output/assertion pass rates — indicating a divergence between correctness-style pass/fail metrics and holistic quality judgments. Many quality comparisons rest on few pairs (1-3) with medium confidence, so these differences should be read as directional signals rather than strong conclusions.

**Runtime/cost:** without_skill frequently shows near-zero runtime and cost (0s, $0.00) in several evals, which combined with missing consistency scores in those same evals raises the possibility that some without_skill runs did not fully execute or were cached/short-circuited rather than reflecting genuinely faster processing — this should be verified rather than read as a pure efficiency win. Where both variants show real runtimes (e.g., symmetric-full-coverage, traffic-engineering, verification-no-fabrication), differences are modest (single-digit to ~10s).

**Output consistency:** Both variants were mostly consistent-to-consistent in most evals; the one exception (without_skill "inconsistent" in supernet-covers-more-specific) stands out as an isolated reliability concern for that specific scenario.

Overall, neither variant dominates cleanly: with_skill shows stronger, more decisive results on verification-no-fabrication and modest edges on hard-gap-single-vif and two-direction-requirement, while without_skill shows stronger results on aggregate-tiling-covered and mixed-but-favorable quality scores elsewhere despite an isolated consistency issue. Several comparisons rest on small sample sizes (1-2 scored pairs) or on assertions that are flaky for both variants, meaning some of these differences are lower-confidence signals rather than firm distinctions.

symmetric-full-coverage.summary:
Both variants performed equivalently on the "objective" measures: the trigger fired in all 3 runs, both without_skill and with_skill met the expected output in 3/3 cases with high confidence, and both passed all 9 assertions (100%) across the three checked behaviors (reports zero gaps, states all prefixes covered on both VIFs, does not invent a gap where prefix sets are identical). Notably, every one of these assertions passed for both variants in every run — meaning none of them differentiate the two systems; they read as solid, established behaviors rather than points of contrast.

Where the variants diverge is in quality comparison and efficiency, and these move in opposite directions. On paired quality judgments (3 pairs evaluated, none skipped), with_skill was favored in 8 of 9 total criterion comparisons (accuracy, actionability, completeness) with 1 rated comparable and zero going to without_skill; this pattern held consistently across all three quality criteria. However, this quality judgment carries only medium average confidence, so it should be treated as a real but not highly certain signal.

On efficiency, without_skill was notably faster and cheaper: ~13s average runtime and $0.11 average cost versus with_skill's ~24s and $0.20 — roughly half the time and cost. Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in any of the 3 evaluated pairs, and context-window utilization was low and similar for both (3.9% vs 4.5%, no compactions for either).

Output consistency was essentially identical between the two: both scored "mostly_consistent" overall with the same numeric score (2.67) and the same dimension breakdown (2 consistent, 1 mostly consistent), both with high confidence — so run-to-run stability is not a distinguishing factor here.

Overall, this is a small eval (3 task instances) where the pass/fail assertions and expected-output checks show no difference between variants, consistency is equivalent, but with_skill tends to produce higher-rated qualitative output (at medium confidence) while without_skill completes tasks faster and at lower cost. This represents a quality-vs-efficiency tradeoff rather than a clear overall difference in capability.

Looking at the three distinct assertion types, both variants passed every one of them 100% of the time whenever evaluated (identifying the 192.168.1.0/24 gap, stating the blackhole consequence, and correctly not flagging the shared 10.10 prefixes). This means none of the individual assertions discriminate between the variants — the difference shows up only in whether without_skill produced a valid/complete response at all in every run, not in the content quality of the assertions checked.

Overall, with_skill was favored in 3 sub-judgments, without_skill in 2, with 1 comparable, at medium average confidence — essentially a mixed/weak signal. Breaking down by criterion: with_skill was favored on completeness (2-0) and split evenly on accuracy (1-1 comparable), while without_skill was favored on actionability (2-0). So each variant shows a distinct strength: with_skill's answers were seen as more complete, without_skill's as more actionable, with accuracy roughly a wash.

Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the 2 pairs evaluated. Context window utilization was low and comparable for both (4.5% vs 3.6%), with no compaction events for either.

Consistency: with_skill's outputs were rated "mostly_consistent" across runs (score 2.67/3, high confidence) with 2 fully consistent and 1 mostly-consistent dimension. No consistency rating is available for without_skill (null), so we cannot compare run-to-run stability directly — this is an absent measurement for without_skill, not a sign of poor consistency.

Overall, the clearest and most confident difference is that without_skill failed to meet the expected output in one of three runs while with_skill met it in all three; assertion-level and quality data are otherwise mixed or too sparse to point to a general quality gap, with each variant showing an edge on a different quality criterion (completeness vs. actionability).
